newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Reforms, privatisation key to Yugoslavia's survival.
newsitem.headline: Reforms, privatisation key to Yugoslavia's survival.

text.p: Yugoslavia must urgently launch privatisation and return to international financial institutions to survive or sink into recession as the last communist stronghold in Europe, experts said on Thursday.

"Europe sees Yugoslavia as the last dark spot on its map where reforms and privatisation have yet to happen," director of the Institute of International Politics and Economics Predrag Simic told Reuters in an interview.
"But with privatisation and reforms it could become a convenient place for foreign capital to compete," he said.
"Without privatisation and renewed ties with the international community, it will be difficult to kick-start the economy. Any transition requires substantial foreign funds," he said.

Six years after the violent break-up of the former Balkan federation, Yugoslavia is still banned from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) barring its return to world markets and blocking foreign investment.
Isolation and further economic decay could tear apart the federation comprising Serbia and Montenegro, analysts said.

"Montenegro is behaving just as Slovenia used to before seceding from Yugoslavia. But Serbia should be more responsive to any Montenegrin criticism to avoid serious consequences," said a political analyst who asked not to be named.
Tiny Montenegro, home to 650,000 people, has been pushing hard for reforms and democracy and out of isolation.
It has demanded from the federal government to urgently fulfil all conditions for dismantling the so-called outer ring of sanctions and Yugoslavia's return to world financial bodies.
The latest in the series of threats coming from Podgorica government included Montenegrin readiness to get access to the IMF and the World Bank independently of Belgrade.
Impatient to wait for Serbia to start reforms, Montenegro has launched its own privatisation model, including voucher privatisation which has been persistently rejected by Belgrade.
But Serbia, accounting for 95 percent of Yugoslav economy and the 10-million population, has been slow to reform.
Analysts said reluctance to reform could be expected in the year of republican elections.
"Reforms have a high social price and privatisation implies massive lay-offs. But a sacked worker is still a voter. And the government cannot afford any social unrest," Simic said.
One year after U.N. sanctions have been suspended, the country has achieved practically no economic progress.
Private economic research institute CES-Mecon said Yugoslavia's gross domestic product (GDP) grew 5.8 percent in 1996 and reached $17 billion.
Industry output rose 7.5 percent, official unemployment stood at 25 percent but unofficially half of the 2.5 million workforce out of work.

Yugoslavia ended 1996 with a $2.26 billion trade gap and a $1.5 billion current account deficit. Inflation was cut down to around 58 percent from 120 in 1995, while the dinar official rate remained unchanged at 3.3 to the German mark.

"All indicators would be encouraging for any other economy, even for Yugoslavia if it was the first year of such economic performance. But Yugoslavia is starting to count its growth from a very low base," CES-Mecon economist Milojko Arsic said.
Idling Yugoslav industries need foreign financial support and technical guidance, preferrably from the United States and the West, analysts said.

"It is important that Yugoslavia identifies its interests close to those of the United States in the region...Without U.S. approval, it will remain outside the IMF for quite some time," the analyst said. -- Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
